---
title: "Why CU"
subtitle: "What a research university brings that others do not"
---

::: {.lead}
CU Boulder would not need to own land or animals to matter here. Its strengths, in environmental science, teaching, and relationships, are exactly what herds run by cities, counties, and Tribal Nations often lack the time or money to provide.
:::

## Research {#research}

Buffalo are one of the few large animals that reshape a whole grassland: how it grazes, burns, stores water and carbon, and supports other wildlife. A herd on a working landscape is a long-term outdoor laboratory, and CU already has the people to use it.

| Question a herd could help answer | CU strengths that apply |
|---|---|
| How does buffalo grazing change grassland plants, soil, and carbon over decades? | Ecology and evolutionary biology; the [Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research (INSTAAR)](https://instaar.colorado.edu/), which runs long-term ecological research |
| How do buffalo, fire, and drought interact as the climate warms? | Climate and earth system science at the [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/) |
| How do grazing patterns affect soil moisture, runoff, and small streams? | Hydrology and geography; satellite and drone monitoring |
| What does Indigenous-led land stewardship look like in practice, and how is it supported well? | Indigenous studies through the [Center for Native American and Indigenous Studies](https://www.colorado.edu/cnais/), working with Tribal partners |

The strongest research would be **designed with Tribal partners**, asking questions they care about and following their rules for how knowledge and data about their lands and relatives are shared.

## Teaching {#teaching}

- **Field courses** on a working grassland within reach of campus, for students in ecology, geography, environmental studies, and Indigenous studies.
- **Student research** that runs for years, so each class builds on the last.
- **Shared learning with Tribal colleges.** CU students and students from Tribal colleges could learn side by side, with Tribal college faculty and knowledge holders teaching as well as learning. That kind of exchange builds pathways to graduate school and careers in both directions.

## Partnerships on the land {#land}

Cities, counties, and federal agencies along the Front Range already manage open space, and two already manage herds. CU would not need to buy land. It could bring science and students to land partners who want them, and help them answer questions they cannot answer alone: is the grassland healthier, is the herd's land enough in a drought year, what does the herd do for wildlife and fire risk.

## Relationships with Tribal Nations {#relationships}

Universities increasingly speak about their relationships with Tribal Nations. A buffalo partnership would be one of the most concrete forms that relationship can take, because:

- Buffalo matter culturally, spiritually, and economically to many Tribal Nations, and returning them to the land is a goal many Nations are already working toward.
- It is long-term by nature. A herd cannot be a one-year initiative.
- It can be shaped by Tribal priorities from the start, rather than asking Tribal Nations to join something already decided.

## What CU would not need to do

- **Own a herd or buy land.** The partnership models include versions where CU contributes no land at all.
- **Lead on cultural matters.** Those decisions belong to Tribal Nations.
- **Start from nothing.** CSU, Denver, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the InterTribal Buffalo Council, and Tribal herds such as Wolakota all have experience CU can learn from.
